benchmark_details.name: Book Advert XML Repair
benchmark_details.overview: Evaluates models on repairing malformed XML markup in transcribed adverts from the Basler Avisblatt (1729–1844), most of them book sale listings tagged for title, author, format and price, while leaving the advert text unchanged.

purpose_and_intended_users.goal: Measure how well language models repair broken XML markup in historical text without altering the text: closing unclosed elements, correcting mismatched tag names and restoring malformed tags, as needed when cleaning the output of automatic tagging pipelines. The results are meant for AI researchers and model developers comparing models on structured-text repair, and for practitioners in digital humanities and editing who post-process semi-structured historical text and choose a model for markup repair.
tasks: preservation of the transcribed text while editing markup
purpose_and_intended_users.limitations:
50 adverts from one newspaper and one tagging scheme. The ground truth makes few changes (none in 11 adverts, one in 30), so returning the input unchanged already scores about 99 of 100 (see Baseline Results) and the range that separates models is narrow; models that repair more than the ground truth, or follow the prompt's invitation to add tags "where it makes sense", lose points.

The ground truth has known defects. Six ground-truth files contain mismatched or unclosed tags (three of them recorded as needing no fixes) and 12 contain an unescaped `&`; the scorer compares character strings, not XML structure, so these go undetected in scoring (see Validation). Mismatched `PRIZE`/`PRICE` pairs are resolved to `PRIZE` in some files and to `PRICE` in others, so the expected repair is not predictable from the input. 49 of 50 texts contain the same encoding damage (UTF-8 read as Mac Roman, e.g. `B√ºcher` for "Bücher"), kept in the ground truth, so a model that also fixes the encoding is penalised. At least one file also corrects an OCR error in the text (`Parabieses` to `Paradieses`) that the prompt does not ask for.
out_of_scope_uses: evaluating XML validation against a schema or DTD
evaluating OCR correction or encoding repair
evaluating tagging of untagged text from scratch

data.source: Adverts from the Basler Avisblatt, the weekly advertising paper of Basel (1729–1844), digitised and processed by the SNSF project "Printed markets: information, data, and news in the Basel 'Avisblatt', 1729–1844" at the University of Basel: https://avisblatt.philhist.unibas.ch/. Most adverts announce books for sale or subscription by booksellers, printers and bookbinders; a few offer other goods. Each is tagged with elements for its bibliographic parts and made malformed.
data.format:
One JSON file per advert under `texts/`, holding the malformed XML as a single string of 66–2,931 characters (median about 1,190):

```json
{
  "xml_string": "<ITEM>11. Bey Herrn Daniel Hag dem Buchbinder sind folgende B√ºcher ... <BIBL><AUTHOR>Ejusd.</AUTHOR> <TITLE>Politicorum Libri</TITLE>. <BIBL><TITLE>Monita</TITLE> ... </ITEM>"
}
```

The ground truth is one JSON file per advert with the repaired string, the number of fixes and an explanation; only `fixed_xml` is scored:

```json
{
  "fixed_xml": "<ITEM>11. Bey Herrn Daniel Hag dem Buchbinder sind folgende B√ºcher ... <BIBL><AUTHOR>Ejusd.</AUTHOR> <TITLE>Politicorum Libri</TITLE>.</BIBL><BIBL><TITLE>Monita</TITLE> ... </ITEM>",
  "number_of_fixes": 3,
  "explanation": "Three closing BIBL tags were missing after the TITLE tags ..."
}
```

Elements used: `ITEM` (one per advert), `BIBL`, `TITLE`, `AUTHOR`, `FORMAT`, `VOLUME`, `YEAR`, `PLACE`, and `PRIZE` or `PRICE` for prices, with single uses of `DAY`, `DATE`, `DESCRIPTION` and `AVAILABILITY`. The ground truth records 0–7 fixes per advert, mostly unclosed `BIBL` or `TITLE` elements and `PRIZE`/`PRICE` tag mismatches.
data.annotation: The repaired ground truth was drafted by a language model and reviewed by the annotator, Sorin Marti, with Ina Serif as domain expert (see Contributors by Role). The source of the malformations (the project's tagging pipeline or deliberate corruption) is not documented. Defects that survived the review are listed under Limitations.
data.collection_date: Source documents: the Avisblatt appeared 1729–1844; the years named in the 50 adverts run up to 1748. Added to the benchmark: December 2025.
data.contamination_controls: None. The texts, prompt and ground truth have been public in this repository since December 2025.

methods: zero-shot repair of one advert per request: the prompt [`prompt.txt`](prompts/prompt.txt) with the advert's JSON file attached

structured JSON output requested with the `CorrectedAdvert` dataclass in all tests but one, which requests no schema; the prompt names the count key `number_of_fixes`, the schema `number_of_corrections`, and neither is scored
output capped at the repository default of 16,384 tokens per request, adjusted per model in `scripts/benchmark_base.py`
methodology.calculation: From the response's `fixed_xml` and the ground truth's `fixed_xml`, all spaces, line feeds and carriage returns are removed; tabs and other whitespace are kept. The advert score is the rapidfuzz `ratio` of the two strings, from 0 to 100. A response that parses but has no `fixed_xml` scores 0. The benchmark score is the unrounded mean of the advert scores. A response that cannot be parsed into the schema is not scored and does not enter the mean.
methodology.interpretation: Scores range from 0 to 100; higher is better. 100 means the strings match after whitespace removal; it does not show that the XML is well-formed. Read scores against the no-edit reference of about 99 (see Baseline Results): a score below it means the model's edits moved the text further from the ground truth than leaving it alone would have. A score covers only the adverts with a parseable response; report the number of scored adverts with it.
methodology.baseline_results:
Model results are on the [benchmark page](https://rise-services.rise.unibas.ch/benchmarks/p/benchmarks/book_advert_xml) and in `results/<date>/<test_id>/` at the repository root. Compare runs with the same prompt, scoring rules and ground-truth revision. No fixed model baseline is defined. Copying each input `xml_string` unchanged into `fixed_xml` scores 99.001739 across the 50 adverts (lowest single advert 84.6).

Observed across models: the task combines syntactic repair, structural reconstruction (adding missing tags) and implicit interpretation (deciding what should be tagged), which blurs what a score measures; separate variants for repair only, repair with enrichment and interpretation-heavy work would allow more controlled comparisons. A single score per advert also hides which kinds of error a model makes; component-level measures such as tag accuracy and hierarchy correctness, and per-sample diagnostics, would make strengths and weaknesses visible.
methodology.validation: The model-drafted ground truth was reviewed by Sorin Marti (see Annotation); no second check is recorded. A strict `xml.etree.ElementTree.fromstring` parse rejects 16 of the 50 ground-truth `fixed_xml` strings (the defects listed under Limitations); this does not affect their string-similarity scores. Scoring is deterministic; the scorer is covered by `tests/test_simple_averagers_scoring.py`.

ethical_and_legal_considerations.privacy_and_anonymity: The adverts name 18th-century booksellers, printers and authors; all are long dead. No living persons are concerned.
ethical_and_legal_considerations.compliance_with_regulations: The advert texts come from the Avisblatt project's published data (Avisdata, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8278751), used under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, the licence in that dataset's rights field (its notes say CC BY-SA 4.0). The adverts were printed in the 18th century and the persons named are long dead, so data protection law does not apply. No separate reuse terms are stated for the ground truth. No ethical review was carried out.
